title: Monolith vs Microservices
description: Understand why you should start with a monolith, when splitting makes sense, and the real operational costs of microservices.

segments.text: Microservices are everywhere in tech conversations. But here's a secret most people won't tell you: starting with microservices is almost always a mistake. Let me show you why.
Meet the monolith — one application, one codebase, one deployment. Everything lives together. It's simple to develop, simple to deploy, simple to debug. One process, one log file, one database.

But as your team and codebase grow, the monolith gets painful. Deploys take an hour. A bug in the payment module crashes the entire app. Ten teams step on each other's code. The monolith becomes a ball of mud.
So at what point does it make sense to split? And more importantly, where do you draw the lines between services?
segments.thought_prompt: What criteria would you use to decide where to split a monolith into separate services?

segments.text: The key is bounded contexts from Domain-Driven Design. Each service should own a clear business capability — orders, payments, inventory. If two pieces of logic change together for the same business reason, they belong in the same service.

Now these services need to talk. Synchronous communication via REST or gRPC is simple but creates coupling. Asynchronous communication via message queues is more resilient but harder to reason about. Most systems use both.

This is crucial: each service must own its own data. No shared databases. If the orders service needs user data, it asks the users service — it doesn't peek into the users database. Shared databases create hidden coupling that defeats the whole purpose.
But wait — if each service has its own database, how do you do a query that joins data across services? Welcome to the hardest problem in microservices.
segments.thought_prompt: How would you query data that lives across multiple microservices with separate databases?

segments.text: Microservices bring serious operational complexity. You need service discovery, distributed tracing, centralized logging, health checks, circuit breakers, deployment pipelines for each service. The infrastructure cost is real.

Network calls fail. Services go down. Messages arrive out of order. Transactions that were one database call in a monolith now span multiple services with saga patterns. Debugging moves from stack traces to distributed traces.

That's why the best advice is: start monolith. Split when you feel the pain. Martin Fowler calls this 'monolith first.' You'll understand your domain better before drawing service boundaries, and you'll avoid premature complexity.

Remember: microservices are not a goal, they're a tool. The goal is independent deployability and team autonomy. If a well-structured monolith gives you that, you don't need microservices. Always weigh the benefits against the distributed systems tax.
